VOC={'A':0,'C':1,'G':2,'T':3}
def encode(s,k):
    v=0
    for ch in s[:k-1]: v=v*4+VOC[ch]
    return v
def kmers(s,k):
    mask=(1<<(2*k))-1
    d=encode(s,k)
    out=d
    for ch in s[k:]:
        out=((out<<2)&mask)+VOC[ch]
        yield out
    return
from collections import defaultdict

report:
## Report: region_006 (region.fasta, 3000 bp)

**Caveat up front:** no external databases (BLAST, Pfam, RepeatMasker) were reachable from this environment, so everything below is *de novo* sequence analysis only.

### Global composition
- **Length 3000 bp, GC 54.9 %.** Base composition is not uniform: A 651, T 702, G 764, C 883 (i.e. **G>C>T>A** — a clear GC skew).
- **Dinucleotide statistics are strongly non-random** (z-scores vs. i.i.d. model): **TA is markedly depleted (z = −5.6)**, while **CG (+5.7)**, **GC (+4.6)** and **TT (+5.8)** are enriched. This TA-poor / CG-and-TT-rich pattern is unusual for mammalian DNA and pushes **CpG O/E to ≈ 1.28 globally**; every 200-bp window across the fragment sits in the 0.86–1.79 range, i.e. the whole 3 kb behaves like one long CpG island.

### Main feature: two long open reading frames on the reverse strand
| ORF | Plus-strand coords | Size | Protein |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ORF-A** | **1484 … 2932** | 1452 nt | **483 aa, ~44.2 kDa**, net charge −15 |
| **ORF-B** | **295 … 1173** | 882 nt | **293 aa, ~27.6 kDa**, net charge −18 |

Both are **complete ATG→stop ORFs on the minus strand**, each with the characteristic family of nested internal ATG start codons (e.g. ORF-A also has alternative starts at nt 2623, 2464, 2320, 2212, 2140, 1996 …, giving shorter 379-, 326-, 278-, 242-, 218-, 170-aa isoforms; ORF-B has starts at 1041, 954, 942, 531 …). They are separated by a ~310-nt intergenic gap (plus-strand **1174 … 1483**).

**Statistical support that this is not just GC-biased noise:** in the reading frame these ORFs occupy (minus-strand frame 1), in-frame stop codons are markedly depleted (19 stops / 999 codons vs. 29 expected; z = −1.94), and the longest stop-free span anywhere is **1032 nt**, which only 1 in 2000 dinucleotide-preserving shuffles of the same sequence reached (**p ≈ 0.0005**). No other frame in either direction shows comparable depletion — in fact the opposite frame of the minus strand is stop-*enriched* (z = +3.31), consistent with a genuine reading frame.

### Secondary observations (weaker)
- Inside ORF-A's span there are two forward-strand ORFs of 108 aa (**1478 … 1801**) and 103 aa (**2283 … 2591**) — i.e. **overlapping opposite-strand coding potential around nt ~1480–1800 and ~2280–2590**. Both are short enough to be ambiguous.
- A local GC trough (**1401 … 1500, 39 % GC** — the lowest 100-bp window in the fragment) sits immediately upstream of ORF-A's start codon at 1484 and contains a single CAAT box (**1450**) and a T₆ tract (**1463–1468**), but no coherent promoter architecture (no −35/−10, no TATA).

### Negative findings
No long internal or terminal inverted repeats, no transposon/LTR-like structure, no G-quadruplexes, no tRNA-like or stem-loop hairpins (exhaustive scan for stems ≥10 bp with ≤1 mismatch found none), no canonical bacterial Shine–Dalgarno leaders, no recognizable protein motifs (Walker A/P-loop, DEAD/DExH box, Rossmann fold, C₂H₂ zinc finger) in either ORF product. Neither protein is predicted transmembrane beyond two marginal hydrophobic stretches in ORF-A (aa 94–112 and 128–146), which are not convincing helices.

### Bottom line
**The one thing that clearly stands out is a pair of long reverse-strand ORFs at nt 295–1173 (293 aa) and nt 1484–2932 (483 aa), backed by frame-specific stop-codon depletion that survives a dinucleotide-preserving shuffle test.** The fragment also shows an unusual global composition (TA-depleted, CpG-rich throughout). Whether these ORFs encode real proteins, and what they do, cannot be determined without a homology search, which was not possible here. Nothing else in the fragment (repeats, structures, motifs) is notable.
